questionText: How do GC latency modes work, and when should you change them?
shortAnswer: Latency modes trade throughput for pause length: Interactive (default, balanced), SustainedLowLatency (no full blocking Gen2 — latency-sensitive apps), Batch (max throughput, longer pauses — background jobs), LowLatency (brief no-GC windows — highly specialized). Change only with measurements, scoped to need.
detailedAnswer: Modes: Batch (server default) favors throughput (concurrent background Gen2, longer pauses acceptable); Interactive (workstation default) favors responsiveness (concurrent + quicker demotions); SustainedLowLatency suppresses full blocking collections (Gen2 induced only — trading eventual memory growth for bounded pauses; trading apps, games, audio); LowLatency blocks all Gen2 during a critical region (try/finally scoped — exceeding the region risks OOM by design!). NoGCRegion (TryStartNoGCRegion): hard guarantee attempt for a byte budget (real-time-ish sections — fails if impossible, plan B required). Rules: measure pause distributions first (GC pause histograms — p99/p999, not averages); scope modes narrowly (SustainedLowLatency app-wide only when the whole app is latency-bound; LowLatency/NoGC only around measured regions with finally-restore); never 'fix' throughput problems with latency modes (they trade, not create); containers share the same knobs (DOTNET_gcServer/latency env). Verification: pause-time improvements with flat-or-better throughput AND bounded memory (SustainedLowLatency grows — watch Gen2 size).
internalWorking: Modes tune background vs blocking collection scheduling and generation budgets (demotion/promotion aggression). SustainedLowLatency defers full blocking GCs (induced collections throw unless forced); NoGCRegion reserves segments up front (allocation beyond budget throws InsufficientMemory — fail-fast by contract).
realWorldUsage: Trading ticks, game loops, audio pipelines, and latency-SLO APIs.
commonMistake: Latency modes for throughput problems (wrong trade), process-wide LowLatency (OOM by design), and NoGCRegion without fallback (hard crashes on budget miss).
technicalConversation: Ask for their pause distribution — p99/p999 numbers (not averages) pick the mode; averages pick nothing.
interviewFollowUp: Why does SustainedLowLatency risk unbounded memory growth, and how do you bound it?
keyTakeaway: Latency modes trade throughput for pauses. Measure p99 first, scope narrowly, watch memory.

questionText: How do you diagnose production .NET issues with dotnet-trace, dotnet-counters, and dotnet-dump?
shortAnswer: Counters for live numbers (GC, JIT, exceptions, threadpool), traces for timelines (CPU stacks, GC events, custom Activity spans), dumps for post-mortem state (heap, threads, locks). Collect remotely, analyze offline — never debug on prod boxes.
detailedAnswer: dotnet-counters monitor (System.Runtime: GC heap size, Gen0/1/2 counts, % Time in GC, threadpool queue/CPU, exceptions/sec, JIT stats; Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting: requests, queue lengths): watch live, alert on thresholds (GC time >5%, queue growth). dotnet-trace collect (default profile + custom providers: Microsoft-Extensions-Logging for logs-as-events, System.Net.Http for calls, your ActivitySources): Speedscope/PerfView flame graphs show hot stacks; GC collection events explain pauses. dotnet-dump collect (full process snapshot on demand or on-crash via DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump) → analyze (clrstack -all (managed stacks per thread — deadlocks visible), dumpheap -stat (type histogram — leak suspects), gcroot (who holds the leak), syncblk (who holds the lock)). Workflow: counters notice → trace locates in time → dump freezes state → analyze offline → fix → verify counters flat. Containers: dotnet-monitor sidecar (authenticated HTTP endpoints for all three — no exec needed). On-crash dumps: DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump=1 + DOTNET_DbgMiniDumpType=Heap (full) with volume (disk!).
codeExample:
# Live numbers:
# dotnet-counters monitor -p <pid> System.Runtime Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting
# Timeline:
# dotnet-trace collect -p <pid> --providers Microsoft-Extensions-Logging:4:5
# Post-mortem:
# dotnet-dump collect -p <pid> && dotnet-dump analyze core_xxx
internalWorking: EventPipe streams runtime events out-of-process (low overhead, always-on capable); counters poll aggregations; dumps suspend + serialize the heap/stacks (full dumps = memory-sized files). SOS commands walk CLR data structures (method tables, sync blocks, EE state).
realWorldUsage: Latency incidents, leak hunts, deadlock autopsies, startup analysis, and CI perf gates.
commonMistake: Debugging on prod (collect, analyze offline!), full dumps without disk plan (disk-full outage), trace without symbols (unreadable stacks — ship PDBs/symbols), and counters without baselines (numbers need normals).
technicalConversation: Ask them to narrate their last incident with these three — notice→locate→freeze→fix is the practiced loop.
interviewFollowUp: When is a dump better than a trace, and vice versa?
keyTakeaway: Counters watch, traces time-travel, dumps freeze. Collect remotely, analyze offline, baseline everything.

questionText: How do you analyze a deadlocked .NET process from a dump?
shortAnswer: Collect a dump, list all managed stacks (clrstack -all), find threads blocked on locks (Monitor.Wait/syncblk owners), trace the wait cycle (A waits B's lock, B waits A's), then fix ordering (global lock order), shrink sections, or remove the lock (concurrent/immutable/message-passing).
detailedAnswer: Steps in dotnet-dump analyze: (1) threads (native + managed mapping, spot the stuck ones — same stack repeated). (2) clrstack -all (find Monitor.Enter/Wait sleeps, semaphore waits, Task.Wait/Result blocks, lock(obj) frames). (3) syncblk (who OWNS each thin lock — owner thread ids). (4) Build the cycle: T1 holds L1 waits L2, T2 holds L2 waits L1 (classic); or pool starvation (all pool threads blocked on one async result — sync-over-async signature: Wait/Result frames everywhere). (5) Fix by class: lock-ordering (global order + documented, or single lock), scope shrink (copy-out-then-process outside), lock removal (Concurrent*/immutable/channels), async-all-the-way (await, never Wait/Result/GetAwaiter().GetResult() on contextful paths), and ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries (frees context capture). Prevention: lock-order documentation + review, lock timeouts (Monitor.TryEnter with timeout + fail-loud — deadlock becomes error, not hang), deadlock detectors in tests (run with timeouts asserting completion), and async analyzers (blocking-call rules). Our stack: async/await end-to-end (no .Result in request paths) is the standing rule.
internalWorking: Monitor thin locks inflate to sync blocks on contention (syncblk table); Wait parks on event queues; threadpool starvation shows all workers blocked with growing queue (counters prove it live). Async deadlocks need a captured SynchronizationContext + blocking wait (ASP.NET classic; Core has no request context — rarer, still possible with custom contexts).
realWorldUsage: Hung APIs/workers, deploy-time freezes, test-suite hangs, and pool-exhaustion incidents.
commonMistake: Restarting without dumps (evidence lost), adding locks to fix locks (more cycles), .Result in async code (the modern classic), and timeout-less waits (hangs instead of errors).
technicalConversation: Ask for their last hang's wait cycle — A-waits-B-waits-A narration (with owner thread ids) is the diagnostic artifact.
interviewFollowUp: Why does lock ordering prevent deadlocks, and what breaks when a new lock joins later?
keyTakeaway: Stacks → owners → cycle → order/shrink/remove. Timeouts turn hangs into errors; async-all-the-way prevents the modern kind.

questionText: How do framework-dependent, self-contained, and single-file deployments compare?
shortAnswer: Framework-dependent: tiny, shares host runtime (fast servicing, needs runtime installed). Self-contained: carries the runtime (~30–150MB, runs anywhere). Single-file: one exe bundling either (extraction or in-memory load). Choose by host control, size budget, and startup needs.
detailedAnswer: Framework-dependent (FDD): kilobytes of app + apphost, runtime from shared install (servers you control, fast security patching centrally, smallest images with runtime base images). Self-contained (SCD): -r win-x64 --self-contained (full runtime copy — runs on bare machines, version-pinned, larger, you service it). Single-file: PublishSingleFile bundles SCD (or FDD subset) into one exe (extraction to temp on first run (startup cost + disk) vs in-memory/embedded (no temp, higher RAM); AV scanners sometimes flag packed exes — allowlist). R2R/AOT compose with all three (startup/size tradeoffs from 06a). Decision: containers → runtime-base FDD or SCD-chiseled (size vs control); desktops/cli → single-file SCD (one artifact, double-clickable); servers you manage → FDD (patch once); locked-down/offline → SCD (no host dependency). Gotchas: native deps (SQLitePCLRaw, Kestrel's QUIC libs ride along — RID-specific!), culture-invariant mode (invariant globalization trims ICU — breaks culture-sensitive code knowingly), event pipe/diagnostics in trimmed singles (include symbols separately), and apphost lookup rules (DOTNET_ROOT, roll-forward).
codeExample:
# Framework-dependent (needs .NET 10 runtime on host):
# dotnet publish -c Release
# Self-contained single file:
# dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained -p:PublishSingleFile=true
# Runtime-base container (small + serviced): FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0
internalWorking: FDD apphost resolves shared framework (roll-forward rules) then loads app assemblies. SCD ships the full host+runtime+framework assemblies (hard-linked dedup in containers). Single-file embeds managed assemblies as resources (loaded via in-memory AssemblyLoadContext or extracted; native libs always extract to temp).
realWorldUsage: Container images, CLI distribution, on-prem installers, and locked-down servers.
commonMistake: SCD without RID (wrong native deps), single-file + Assembly.Location assumptions (empty/extracted paths — use AppContext.BaseDirectory), and FDD on hosts without the runtime (the classic 'you must install .NET' incident).
technicalConversation: Ask what ships and what runs it — artifact + host contract (runtime present? who patches?) decides the mode.
interviewFollowUp: Why do native dependencies complicate single-file, and how do RIDs resolve it?
keyTakeaway: FDD shares, SCD carries, single-file bundles. Match artifact to host control and servicing.

questionText: How do AppContext switches and runtime knobs provide compatibility escapes?
shortAnswer: AppContext.SetSwitch / runtimeconfig / DOTNET_ env vars toggle runtime behaviors (compat quirks, GC flavors, globalization, threading) without code changes — the supported escape hatches for version-behavior deltas. Use sparingly, document why, revisit each upgrade.
detailedAnswer: Shape: AppContext.SetSwitch("System.Net.Http.UseSocketsHttpHandler", false) (code), runtimeconfig.json runtimeOptions.configProperties (deploy-time), DOTNET_SYSTEM_* env (ops-time, containers). Common knobs: GC flavors (Server/Workstation, latency, heap limits DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit — container memory compliance!), globalization invariant mode, threadpool min threads (burst readiness), TieredCompilation/PGO toggles (perf experiments), SocketsHttpHandler vs WinHttpHandler (proxy/TLS edge cases), EF query behaviors (split-query defaults, sensitive logging). Discipline: one switch per documented reason (link the issue), test both positions (switch-dependent code paths need dual coverage), audit per upgrade (quirks get removed — switches rot into no-ops or errors), and prefer code fixes (switches are bridges, not homes). Discovery: runtime docs 'runtime configuration options' reference + release-note breaking-change sections (each names its switch). Containers: env knobs beat baked config (same image, tuned per environment).
internalWorking: Switches read once at runtime init (most are startup-only — changing later has no effect; a few poll). Env > runtimeconfig > code-defaults precedence (ops overrides deploy overrides code). GC heap limits reshape segment sizing; threadpool mins pre-create workers.
realWorldUsage: Container tuning, upgrade firefighting (quirk toggles), perf experiments, and globalization edge cases.
commonMistake: Switches as permanent fixes (rot + tech debt), startup-only switches changed at runtime (silent no-op), and untested switch positions (the untested path breaks at 3am).
technicalConversation: Ask which knobs their containers set — none (defaults under memory limits = OOM kills) versus tuned heap/thread settings is the ops maturity gap.
interviewFollowUp: Why are most runtime switches startup-only, and what does that imply for hot-tuning?
keyTakeaway: Switches bridge version deltas, not design gaps. Document, dual-test, revisit per upgrade.

questionText: How does TimeProvider make time testable, and what patterns replace DateTime.Now/UtcNow?
shortAnswer: TimeProvider abstracts clocks (GetUtcNow, timestamps, timers); inject it (or TimeProvider.System default), use FakeTimeProvider in tests for deterministic time travel. Replace all direct DateTime.UtcNow/Task.Delay with provider calls — untestable time is the #1 flaky-test source.
detailedAnswer: Patterns: ctor-inject TimeProvider (default = TimeProvider.System — zero ceremony: ctor(TimeProvider? clock = null) { this.clock = clock ?? TimeProvider.System; }); use clock.GetUtcNow()/GetTimestamp() for stamps, clock.CreateTimer for callbacks, Task.Delay(interval, ct) stays (cancellation-driven, not clock-driven — fine). Tests: FakeTimeProvider (Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing) — Advance(TimeSpan) deterministically fires timers/delays (no Thread.Sleep, no flakiness): cache-expiry tests advance 11 minutes instantly; scheduler tests step ticks. PeriodicTimer accepts TimeProvider (.NET 8+: new PeriodicTimer(span, timeProvider) — deterministic ticks!). Migration: DateTime.UtcNow → _clock.GetUtcNow().UtcDateTime (mechanical), Task.Delay stays (token-driven), Stopwatch → GetTimestamp/ GetElapsedTime (monotonic, fakeable). What NOT to fake: timeouts driven by cancellation (use CTS with test timeouts), wall-clock display (pass through — display isn't logic). Singletons: TimeProvider.System shared (thread-safe, stateless) — no lifetime concerns.
internalWorking: TimeProvider.GetUtcNow reads the system clock (or fake's manual value); timers schedule against provider time (fake advances fire synchronously — no threads). PeriodicTimer(timeProvider) binds ticks to fake advancement (deterministic scheduling in tests).
realWorldUsage: Expiry logic, schedulers, retry backoffs, rate windows, and SLA timers.
commonMistake: DateTime.Now in logic (untestable + local-time bugs — UtcNow minimum, provider preferred), Thread.Sleep in tests (slow + flaky), and faking display clocks (noise — fake logic clocks only).
technicalConversation: Ask how their expiry tests work — Sleep-based (slow/flaky) versus FakeTimeProvider (instant/deterministic) reveals test maturity.
interviewFollowUp: Why is Task.Delay acceptable without a provider while DateTime.UtcNow is not?
keyTakeaway: Inject TimeProvider, fake it in tests, travel instantly. Untestable time is flaky suites.

questionText: How do you correlate logs, traces, and metrics for a single incident end to end?
shortAnswer: One TraceId everywhere (W3C Activity → log scopes → metric exemplars), one backend family (or correlated exporters), one timeline view. During incidents: alert fires from metrics, traces show the path, logs show the state — same id joins all three.
detailedAnswer: Setup: ASP.NET + HttpClient + EF auto-instrumentation (Activities with TraceIds), ILogger scope enrichment (TraceId/SpanId on every event — OTel logging does this), metrics with trace-exemplars (hot histogram buckets link to exemplar traces). Flow: Alert (burn-rate on latency/errors) → exemplar trace (the slow/failing request's full path with timings per span) → logs filtered to that TraceId (state, decisions, payloads-scrubbed) → fix → verify (same dashboards green). Practices: consistent service/resource names (service.name/version/instance — cardinality-safe), baggage for tenant/flags (propagated, low-cardinality only!), tail sampling keeping all errors (100% errors, 1% success — errors never sampled away), and retention aligned (traces ≥ incident-review window). Anti-patterns: separate ids per signal (unjoinable), trace ids in metrics tags (cardinality bomb — exemplars instead), logs without ids (archaeology), and three backends that can't cross-link (one pane or deep links). Drills: game-day with a known TraceId (can the on-call walk all three in <5 min?).
internalWorking: W3C traceparent propagates (ActivityContext parse/inject at client/server instrumentation); OTel logging stamps TraceId/SpanId from current Activity; exemplars attach (traceId, spanId) to histogram buckets (Prometheus/OpenMetrics native). Samplers decide per-trace at root (consistent decision propagated downstream).
realWorldUsage: Multi-service incidents, latency attribution, error forensics, and SLO reviews.
commonMistake: Unjoined signals (three pagers, no thread), trace ids as metric tags (cardinality explosion), 100% sampling (cost), and missing tail rules (errors sampled away — the worst loss).
technicalConversation: Ask them to walk one recent incident across all three signals with a single id — gaps in the walk are the observability roadmap.
interviewFollowUp: Why do exemplars beat trace-id tags on metrics?
keyTakeaway: One TraceId joins metrics (alert), traces (path), logs (state). Sample tails, tag lean, drill the walk.

questionText: What is the difference between Random, RandomNumberGenerator, and Guid for identifiers and security?
shortAnswer: Random = fast, non-crypto PRNG (simulations, shuffling, test data — seedable, NOT thread-safe instances). RandomNumberGenerator = OS CSPRNG (tokens, salts, keys — use it). Guid v4 = unique ids (not randomness — never for secrets). Shuffle with Random.Shared (thread-safe); secrets with RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes/GetInt32.
detailedAnswer: Random: deterministic algorithm (seeded — same seed, same sequence: great for reproducible tests/simulations); instance methods are NOT thread-safe (shared instance across threads corrupts state → zeros/duplicates — use Random.Shared, thread-safe via striped instances). RandomNumberGenerator (System.Security.Cryptography): BCryptGenRandom/getrandom-backed (blocking-quality entropy, thread-safe, disposes nothing — static methods preferred: GetBytes(span), GetInt32(max), GetString(alphabet, length) for OTPs). Guid.NewGuid: unique (v4 random bits, but not a CSPRNG contract + version/variant bits reduce entropy — uniqueness, not secrecy; predictable after state leaks). Rules: tokens/passwords/salts/nonces → RandomNumberGenerator; simulations/shuffling/sampling → Random/Shared; public ids → Guid/UUIDv7 (sortable!); test determinism → seeded Random (repeatable failures). ASP.NET: DataProtection for tokens-at-rest (purpose-bound encryption, not raw randomness). Pitfalls: new Random() per call (same-tick seeds → identical sequences — the classic duplicate 'random' codes!), Guid substring as password (low entropy + predictable), and modulo bias (use GetInt32, not % on bytes).
internalWorking: Random is xoshiro256** (fast, period 2^256, seedable state). RandomNumberGenerator calls OS entropy (getrandom/BCryptGenRandom — syscalls, slower, non-reproducible). Random.Shared stripes per-thread instances. GetInt32 uses rejection sampling (no modulo bias).
realWorldUsage: Session/OTP tokens, password salts, id generation, load-test data, shuffles, and sampling.
commonMistake: new Random() in a loop (identical seeds → identical 'random'), Guid as secret (predictable + low entropy), shared Random across threads (corruption), and % bias on crypto bytes (use GetInt32).
technicalConversation: Ask where their tokens come from — GetBytes/GetInt32 (correct) versus Guid-substring or new-Random (findings).
interviewFollowUp: Why is new Random() per call dangerous, and what does Random.Shared do differently?
keyTakeaway: CSPRNG for secrets, Random for speed/simulations, Guid for uniqueness. Seed for tests, share safely.

questionText: How do source-generated logging (LoggerMessage) and regex generators improve hot paths?
shortAnswer: LoggerMessageAttribute generates zero-allocation, skip-if-disabled logging methods (no parsing, no boxing, no closure); GeneratedRegexAttribute compiles patterns at build time (no startup cost, trimmable). Both move work from runtime to compile time — use on any hot or AOT path.
detailedAnswer: LoggerMessage: [LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Information, Message = "Order {OrderId} placed")] static partial void OrderPlaced(ILogger logger, int orderId); — generated code checks IsEnabled first (zero cost when off), skips template parsing (prebuilt callback), avoids boxing value types (typed overloads), and works in AOT (no reflection). Rules: static partial in static or instance partial class, ILogger first param, message template with matching param names, EventId/EventName for categorization (alert routing!). GeneratedRegex: [GeneratedRegex(@"^\d{3}-\d{4}$")] static partial Regex Phone(); — compile-time MSIL + DFA analysis (invalid patterns fail the BUILD, options like IgnoreCase baked in), trimmable/AOT-safe (no runtime compilation), 2–5x faster than new Regex + thread-safe static. When: hot-path logs (request lines, loop events), validation regexes (emails, SKUs, routes), and AOT apps (both required for trimming). Testing: assert generated behavior identically (same cases as before — generation changes mechanics, not semantics); build breaks on bad patterns (good — fail fast). Migration: highest-volume Log* calls first (profile-guided), then validation regexes; leave cold paths idiomatic.
internalWorking: LoggerMessage generator emits IsEnabled check + strongly-typed logging call-site (no params array for common arities — no allocation). Regex generator emits a custom Regex-derived class with unrolled matching code (DFA→source), validated at compile time (ReGenerator diagnostics on unsupported constructs).
realWorldUsage: Hot request/event logs, input validators, route parsers, and AOT-trimmed apps.
commonMistake: Partial-method signature mismatches (build error — read it), template/param name drift (build error — good), applying to cold paths (noise — profile first), and dynamic patterns (generators need constants — runtime-built regex stays runtime).
technicalConversation: Ask which logs fire per request — those call sites are the LoggerMessage candidates; profile confirms the allocation win.
interviewFollowUp: Why do generated loggers stay zero-alloc when disabled while interpolation does not?
keyTakeaway: Generate hot logging and regexes at build time: zero runtime parsing, AOT-safe, build-caught errors.

questionText: How do decorators and Scrutor extend the built-in DI container, and when are they worth it?
shortAnswer: MS.DI has no built-in decorator support — Scrutor adds assembly scanning + Decorate<TService, TDecorator> (explicit stacking). Worth it for cross-cutting chains (caching/logging/retry around repositories/gateways); skip for one-offs (hand-wire those).
detailedAnswer: Without Scrutor, decoration is manual descriptor surgery (Replace with a factory closure — verbose, order-fragile). Scrutor: services.Decorate<IOrders, CachedOrders>().Decorate<IOrders, LoggedOrders>() — registration-order stacking (outermost last), open generics supported (Decorate(typeof(IRepo<>), typeof(CachedRepo<>))), plus Scan for convention registration (FromAssemblyOf<T>().AddClasses(c => c.Where(t => t.Name.EndsWith("Service"))).AsImplementedInterfaces().WithScopedLifetime() — kills 50-line registration blocks). Lifetime fidelity: decorators inherit the decorated lifetime (scoped stays scoped — no captive surprises when stacked consistently). Testing: assert the chain (resolve IOrders, assert outermost type + behavior with fakes inside). Costs: extra package + magic-by-convention (scanning surprises — explicit scans with narrow filters), stack-trace depth (+N frames per decorator — name well), and debug indirection (decoratee hidden — log the chain at startup in dev). Alternatives: MediatR pipeline behaviors (cross-cutting around handlers — often cleaner than service decorators), middleware/filters (request-scoped concerns), and manual factories for singletons-with-parameters. Our codebase: hand-rolled explicit registrations fit current scale (Scrutor-worthy at ~5+ decorators or scanning payoff).
internalWorking: Decorate rewrites descriptors into factory closures (inner resolved from a child scope view — lifetime preserved by construction). Scanning emits descriptors at startup (one-time reflection cost; trimmable concerns for AOT — prefer explicit in trimmed apps).
realWorldUsage: Repository caching/logging/retry chains, gateway resilience stacks, and convention-based feature-module registration.
commonMistake: Unordered decoration (outermost confusion — registration order IS the order), scanning too broadly (unintended registrations — narrow filters), and decorators around disposables (ownership — container still owns the graph).
technicalConversation: Ask how their cross-cutting currently composes — base classes (fragile), manual wrappers (verbose), or decorators (explicit chains).
interviewFollowUp: Why do decorators preserve lifetime fidelity while manual singletons-around-scoped break it?
keyTakeaway: Scrutor = explicit decoration + convention scanning. Chains for cross-cutting, manual for one-offs.
